early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It typically affects older leaves first, causing dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern).
symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with concentric rings on older leaves
Yellow halo surrounding the spots
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Stem lesions near soil level in severe cases
treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides (e.g., Copper Oxychloride) every 7-10 days
Use chlorothalonil or mancozeb fungicide sprays
Remove and destroy infected leaves immediately
Apply neem oil spray as an organic alternative
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and resistant varieties
Practice crop rotation (avoid planting tomatoes in the same spot for 2-3 years)
Maintain proper plant spacing for good air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation instead
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash

late_blight.description: Late blight is a devastating disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions and can destroy entire crops within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale green to brown lesions on leaves
White fuzzy mold on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Dark brown lesions on stems
Fruit shows brown, firm rot
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides like metalaxyl or mefenoxam immediately
Use protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) preventively
Remove and destroy all infected plant material
Apply phosphorous acid-based products for organic control
prevention: Plant resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Legend, Defiant)
Ensure good drainage and air circulation
Monitor weather forecasts and apply fungicides before wet periods
Destroy volunteer potato and tomato plants

leaf_mold.description: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva). It thrives in high humidity and primarily affects greenhouse tomatoes.
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mold on lower leaf surface
Leaves curl, wither, and drop
Rarely affects fruit but can cause blossom drop
treatment: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil or copper
Improve ventilation in greenhouses
Reduce humidity by adjusting irrigation timing
Remove heavily infected leaves
prevention: Ensure good air circulation between plants

septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is one of the most common tomato diseases and primarily attacks foliage.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark brown borders and gray-white centers
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in the center of spots
Yellowing of leaves around the spots
Severe defoliation starting from lower leaves
treatment: Apply fungicides with chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper
Remove infected leaves at first sign of disease
Apply organic copper-based sprays
Use biofungicides containing Bacillus subtilis
prevention: Rotate crops for at least 2 years
Stake plants to improve air circulation
Remove plant debris at end of season

bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species. It affects leaves, stems, and fruits, causing significant yield loss in warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves
Spots may have a yellow halo
Raised, scab-like lesions on fruit
Severe defoliation in advanced stages
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides early in the season
Use streptomycin sprays in severe cases (where permitted)
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
prevention: Use pathogen-free certified seeds and transplants
Sanitize tools and equipment between plants

target_spot.description: Target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It causes circular lesions with concentric rings on leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, brown circular spots with light centers on leaves
Concentric rings within spots (target-board appearance)
Spots may merge, causing large necrotic areas
Premature defoliation
treatment: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil or azoxystrobin
Remove infected leaves promptly
Apply neem oil as an organic alternative
prevention: Ensure good air circulation between plants
Rotate crops and remove debris at end of season

yellow_leaf_curl_virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). It causes stunting and severe yield loss.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaves
Yellowing of leaf margins
Stunted plant growth
Reduced fruit set and small fruit
treatment: No chemical cure — manage the whitefly vector
Apply imidacloprid or thiamethoxam insecticides for whiteflies
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Use reflective mulch to repel whiteflies
prevention: Control whitefly populations with sticky traps
Remove weeds that can host whiteflies

mosaic_virus.description: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly stable virus transmitted mechanically through contaminated tools, hands, and seeds.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf curling and distortion
Stunted growth
Reduced and uneven fruit ripening
treatment: No chemical treatment available for viral infections
Remove and destroy infected plants
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach or trisodium phosphate
prevention: Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants
Avoid smoking near plants (tobacco mosaic virus cross-infection)

spider_mites.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny arachnids that feed on plant cells, causing stippling and bronzing of leaves.
symptoms: Fine stippling (tiny yellow or white dots) on leaf surfaces
Bronzing or yellowing of leaves
Fine webbing on undersides of leaves
Leaf drop in severe infestations
treatment: Spray with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil
Apply miticides (abamectin, bifenthrin) for severe infestations
Use neem oil spray as organic control
Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
prevention: Maintain adequate watering — drought stress increases mite populations
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators
Wash plants with a strong water spray to dislodge mites

healthy.description: The tomato plant appears healthy with no signs of disease. Continue regular care and monitoring.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and vibrant
treatment: No treatment required
Continue regular watering and fertilization schedule
prevention: Monitor for early signs of pests or disease

early_blight.description: Potato early blight is caused by Alternaria solani. It affects leaves, stems, and tubers, reducing yield significantly.
symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings on leaves
Yellowing of tissue surrounding lesions
Lesions on stems appear dark and sunken
Tubers show dark, sunken lesions with corky texture
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin) at first sign
Remove and destroy infected plant material
Apply copper-based fungicides as organic option
prevention: Maintain adequate soil fertility (avoid nitrogen deficiency)

late_blight.description: Potato late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans is the most destructive potato disease, responsible for the Irish Potato Famine of the 1840s.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown-black
White sporulation on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Rapid collapse of foliage
Tubers show reddish-brown rot under skin
treatment: Apply metalaxyl, cymoxanil, or dimethomorph fungicides immediately
Destroy infected haulm before harvest
Apply phosphorous acid for organic management
prevention: Use resistant varieties (e.g., Sarpo Mira, Cara)
Apply preventive fungicides during high-risk weather

healthy.description: The potato plant appears healthy with no signs of disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and vibrant
treatment: No treatment required

brown_spot.description: Rice brown spot is caused by the fungus Cochliobolus miyabeanus. It is a major disease that can cause significant yield losses, especially in nutrient-deficient soils.
symptoms: Oval to circular brown spots on leaves with gray or whitish centers
Dark brown borders around spots
Spots on glumes (husks) causing discoloration
Seedling blight in severe cases
treatment: Apply fungicides like iprodione, propiconazole, or tricyclazole
Apply potassium and silicon fertilizers to strengthen plants
Treat seeds with thiram or captan before planting
prevention: Treat seeds with hot water (52°C for 10 minutes)

bacterial_blight.description: Rice bacterial blight caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae is one of the most serious rice diseases worldwide, particularly in Asia.
symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish stripe on leaf margins
Lesions turn yellow to white as they enlarge
Wilting of seedlings (kresek phase) in severe cases
Milky or opaque bacterial ooze on cut leaf ends
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides
Drain fields and reduce nitrogen application
No highly effective chemical control — focus on prevention
Apply zinc sulfate to boost plant immunity
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (IR64, IR72, IRRI varieties)

leaf_smut.description: Rice leaf smut is caused by the fungus Entyloma oryzae. It is a minor disease but can cause cosmetic damage to leaves.
symptoms: Small, angular, black spots on leaf blades and sheaths
Spots are slightly raised with a sooty appearance
Affected leaves may turn yellow
Rarely causes significant yield loss
treatment: Apply propiconazole or hexaconazole fungicides
Remove and destroy infected plant material
Improve field drainage

healthy.description: The rice plant appears healthy with no signs of disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and vibrant
treatment: No treatment required

common_rust.description: Corn common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It is widespread and can cause significant yield losses in susceptible varieties.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongated powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules are cinnamon-brown to dark brown in color
Severe infection causes leaves to yellow and die
Pustules rupture to release reddish-brown spores
treatment: Apply fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) at early disease stages
Use propiconazole or azoxystrobin-based products
Apply at VT (tasseling) stage for best results
prevention: Plant early to avoid peak rust season
Monitor fields regularly during warm, humid weather
Rotate crops to reduce inoculum levels

northern_leaf_blight.description: Northern leaf blight (NLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It is a major foliar disease of corn in temperate regions.
symptoms: Long, elliptical gray-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions 2.5-15 cm long with wavy margins
Dark green, water-soaked borders on young lesions
Severe infection causes premature death of leaves
treatment: Apply fungicides (azoxystrobin, propiconazole, pyraclostrobin) at early stages
Apply at tasseling (VT) to silking (R1) stage
Foliar applications most effective when disease is below the ear leaf
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids with Ht genes
Rotate with non-host crops (soybeans, small grains)
Till crop residue to reduce inoculum
Avoid planting in fields with history of severe NLB

gray_leaf_spot.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is one of the most significant foliar diseases of corn in warm, humid environments.
symptoms: Small, rectangular, tan to gray lesions on leaves
Lesions are bounded by leaf veins, giving a rectangular shape
Lesions may coalesce, causing large areas of dead tissue
Mature lesions appear gray due to sporulation
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides (pyraclostrobin, azoxystrobin) at VT-R1 stages
Use triazole fungicides (propiconazole) for preventative treatment
Apply when disease reaches lower canopy
prevention: Till crop residue to reduce overwintering inoculum

healthy.description: The corn plant appears healthy with no signs of disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and vibrant
treatment: No treatment required
